title: Operating systems
description: Scheduling, deadlocks, paging, semaphores and threads: the OS questions that come up in technical interviews.

resources.title: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces (free book)

questions.prompt: Which CPU scheduling algorithm can make long jobs wait forever (starvation) when short jobs keep arriving?
questions.explanation: SJF always picks the shortest waiting job, so a steady stream of short jobs can keep a long one waiting indefinitely. Ageing (raising priority over time) is the usual fix. FCFS and round robin serve every job eventually.

questions.prompt: Which of these is **not** one of the four necessary conditions for deadlock?
questions.explanation: The four conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, **no** preemption, and circular wait. Allowing preemption breaks one of them, which is a way to prevent deadlock.

questions.prompt: A system is thrashing. What is it spending most of its time on?
options: Moving pages between memory and disk
questions.explanation: Thrashing happens when processes don't have enough frames for their working sets, so they page fault constantly and the CPU mostly waits for paging I/O.

questions.prompt: A system uses 32-bit virtual addresses and 4 KB pages. How many bits of an address are the page offset?
questions.explanation: 4 KB = 4,096 = 2¹² bytes, so 12 bits select a byte within a page. The remaining 20 bits are the page number.

questions.prompt: What does a context switch save so that a process can resume later?
options: Its CPU state: registers, program counter and stack pointer
The process's whole memory, to disk
questions.explanation: The kernel saves the CPU state into the process control block and loads the next process's state. Memory stays where it is.

questions.prompt: A counting semaphore starts at 3. Five `wait()` (P) operations and then two `signal()` (V) operations are performed. What is its value at the end?
questions.explanation: 3 − 5 + 2 = 0. In implementations that allow negative values, it goes 3 → −2 → 0. In ones that block at 0, two processes wait and the two signals wake them, leaving 0 either way.

questions.prompt: Belady's anomaly, where adding more frames causes more page faults, can happen with which page replacement algorithm?
questions.explanation: FIFO can fault more with more frames. LRU and the optimal algorithm are stack algorithms: the pages in memory with k frames are always a subset of those with k + 1 frames, so they never show the anomaly.

questions.prompt: Threads of the same process share which of these?
questions.explanation: Threads share the process's address space: code, heap, globals and open files. Each thread has its own stack, registers and program counter.

questions.prompt: Round robin scheduling with a very large time quantum behaves like which algorithm?
questions.explanation: If the quantum is longer than any burst, every process runs to completion in arrival order: that's FCFS.

questions.prompt: Which memory scheme suffers from **external** fragmentation?
questions.explanation: Variable-size holes appear between allocations, so free memory can be split into pieces too small to use. Paging avoids external fragmentation (it can waste part of the last page instead: internal fragmentation).
